title: The spring equinox
hookLine: day and night equal: an image of balance

cards: Twice a year, the sun, as seen from Earth, crosses the line of the equator, and for a day the whole planet, from Oslo to Cape Town, gets roughly the same amount of light and dark. Twelve hours, give or take.
In March, for the northern half of the world, the light is winning from here on.
Many peoples have marked it: Nowruz, the Persian new year, begins at that moment, and the date of Easter is still reckoned from a spring equinox fixed at March 21.
Today the porch looks at the spring equinox as a picture of balance.

teach.b: First, the word. Equinox comes from Latin, aequinoctium: equal night. And a small surprise: it isn't exactly equal.
Because the sun is a disk, not a point, and the air bends its light, most places get a few minutes more day than night on the equinox itself; the truly equal day comes a little before it in spring.
Balance in nature is close, not perfect. Second, the Stoic picture. Seneca, writing to his friend Serenus about peace of mind, lists alternations.

teach.h: SOLITUDE AND COMPANY, WORK AND REST.
teach.b: Mix solitude and company: being alone makes us long for people, people make us long to be alone, and each cures the other.

Give the mind rest, the way you'd let a field lie fallow, because ground forced to produce every year wears out. He mentions that Socrates wasn't ashamed to play with small children. Third, what balance isn't.
It isn't a perfect fifty-fifty schedule, like the equinox that's never quite exact.
It's noticing which way you've tipped: too much work, not enough rest; too many people, not enough quiet; too much screen, not enough sky.

teach.h: CHECK BEFORE THE LIGHT RUNS AWAY.
teach.b: Fourth, why spring is a good time to check. Things are about to grow fast. Days lengthen.
Before the light runs away with you, the equinox stands still for a day and shows you what even looks like.

how: Many cultures mark the spring equinox with new-year or spring festivals; some people use it as a moment to look at the balance of work, rest and company in their lives.

o: Latin for the first warm day after the long winter
Latin for the sun's highest point in the summer sky
Latin for equal night, the root of our word equinox

s: on the equinox, day and night are exactly twelve hours everywhere
most places get a few minutes more day; the sun is a disk and the air bends light.
Seneca advised mixing solitude with company
being alone makes us long for people, and people make us long to be alone.
Seneca thought the mind should work without rest
he compared a rested mind to a field left fallow.

games.q: you've worked straight through for weeks and feel worn down. what does Seneca recommend?
o: push harder until the work is done
give the mind rest, like a fallow field
games.why: in On Tranquility of Mind he says ground forced to produce without a break wears out; the mind needs rest too.

practice: Picture your ordinary day as a scale: work, errands, screens and people on one side; rest, quiet, play and time outside on the other.
See which side hangs lower, without scolding yourself, and choose one small thing to move across: ten minutes of quiet, a walk without your phone, a call to a friend if you've been alone too much.
Picture the scale shifting, just slightly.

wordCard.voice: Aequinoctium, Latin for equal night, the root of the word equinox, when day and night come close to even. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: equal night, the root of equinox.

carryVoice: Your line: equal light. Close to even is as even as nature gets. Until tomorrow.

sources.work: Seneca, On Tranquility of Mind (De Tranquillitate Animi)
